title.title: More on the fractional chromatic number

editorial_contributions.text: There are two well-known ways of defining the fractional chromatic number of a graph \(G\). One of them defines this parameter as the infimum of a certain linear program, the other makes use of set colorings of \(G\). In this note the author discusses the relationship of these two definitions and shows that they are equivalent if the fractional chromatic number of \(G\) is finite. Finally, he lists several interesting open problems with a particular emphasis on infinite graphs.

editorial_contributions.text: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \((v_1,v_2, \dots)\) be an ordering of its vertices. A greedy colouring of \(G\) colours the vertices of \(G\) by colours \(0,1,2, \dots\) in the order listed, and at the \(i\)th stage, the colour of \(v_i\) is defined to be the smallest colour not occurring on any neighbour of \(v_i\). The authors define the Grundy number \(\Gamma(G)\) of \(G\) to be the maximum, over all greedy colourings, of the number of colours used. It is easy to see that \(\Gamma(G)\leq\Delta(G)+1\), where \(\Delta(G)\) denotes the maximum degree of \(G\). The main result of the paper is that for the Grundy number of the \(n\)-dimensional cube \(Q_n\) one has \(\Gamma(Q_2)=2\) and \(\Gamma(Q_n) =n+1\), otherwise.

title.title: Graphs which are vertex-critical with respect to the edge-chromatic number

editorial_contributions.text: The edge-chromatic number of graph G is denoted by \(\chi '(G)\). A multigraph G is EN-critical (VN-critical) if it is connected, Class 2, and \(\chi '(G-e)<\chi '(G)\) for all edges e in G \((\chi '(G-v)<\chi '(G)\) for all vertices v in G). A multigraph G is EC-critical (VC-critical) if it is connected, Class 2, and G-e is Class 1 for all e in G (G-v is Class 1 for all v in G). For simple graphs EN-critical and EC-critical are equivalent. In this paper a number of interesting results and conjectures are given regarding multigraphs which are EN-critical but not EC- critical, regarding the relationship between VN-critical and VC-critical graphs and the relationship between VC-critical and EC-critical graphs.

For an Abelian group \((A,+,0)\) with \(S\subseteq A\) the set S is called weakly two-free if \(\sum^{k}_{i=1}m_ is_ i\neq 0\) whenever \(s_ 1,...,s_ k\in S\) and \(m_ 1,...,m_ k\) are integers such that \(\sum^{k}_{i=1}m_ i\) is odd (*). A coloring of A forbids S if and only if, for all \(a\in A\) and \(s\in S\), a and \(a+s\) have different colors (**). Let \(G=G(A,S)\) be the Cayley graph, whose vertices are in A, and in which a,b\(\in A\) are adjacent if and only if a-b\(\in S\cup (-S).\) 


Then (*) says that S is weakly two-free if and only if there is no walk of odd length in G starting and ending at 0. Definition (**) says that a coloring of A forbids S if it is an admissible vertex-coloring of G. The content of the paper is the proof of the following theorem: 


Suppose that m is a squarefree positive integer, and \(m\equiv 1\) mod 4 or \(m\equiv 2\) mod 4. Then [Q(\(\sqrt{m})]\) 2 is two-colorable so that all the distances \(\sqrt{p/q}\), p, q odd positive integers, are forbidden. 


Further, the author poses some problems arising from this theorem.

editorial_contributions.text: The upper chromatic number of a metric space \((X,d)\) is the smallest positive integer \(m\) such that for each sequence \(s_1,\dots, s_m> 0\) there is a partition of \(X\) into sets \(X_1,\dots, X_m\) (here allowed to be empty) such that no two points of \(X_i\) are a distance \(s_i\) apart, \(i= 1,\dots, m\). The authors promote the study of another sequence of forbidden-distance chromatic numbers related to the upper chromatic numbers, but seemingly much more tractable: for \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and metric space \((X,d)\), \(B_k(X)\) is the smallest \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) (if any) such that for every set of \(k\) or fewer positive numbers, there is a coloring of \(X\) with \(m\) colors with every distance in the set forbidden for every color.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The chromatic number has a well-known interpretation in the area of scheduling. If the vertices of a finite, simple graph are committees, and adjacency of two committees indicates that they must never be in session simultaneously, then the chromatic number of the graph is the smallest number of hours during which the committees/vertices of the graph may all have properly scheduled meetings of one continuous hour each. \textit{T. Slivnik} [Extremal problems for cliques and colorings. Cambridge: University of Cambridge (PhD Thesis)  (1996)] showed that the fractional chromatic number can be similarly characterized. In that characterization, the meetings are allowed to be broken into a finite number of disjoint intervals. \par Here we consider chromatic numbers definable similarly, with the additional restriction that there are only $k$ meeting rooms available; that is, at each instant no more than $k$ committees can be in session.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: A graph is Hall \(t\)-chromatic if there is a proper list-multicoloring of the graph from a constant list of cardinality \(t\) whenever the graph together with that constant list assignment and the ``color demand'' function that prescribes the cardinalities of the color sets, satisfy Hall's condition. We show that every graph is Hall \(t\)-chromatic for \(t\leq 2\), and that a great many familiar graphs, including the bipartite graphs and the complete multipartite graphs, are Hall \(t\)-chromatic for all \(t\). However, it turns out that there exist graphs that are not Hall \(t\)-chromatic for all \(t\) sufficiently large.

title.title: Hall \(t\)-chromatic graphs

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Hall's condition on a finite simple graph equipped with a vertex list assignment and a ``color demand'' function is a necessary condition for the existence of a proper vertex multicoloring satisfying certain requirements. Hall's \(t\)-condition is Hall's condition particularized to the cases when the list assignment is constant. A graph is Hall \(t\)-chromatic if, for every color demand function on it, the satisfying of Hall's \(t\)-condition suffices for the existence of a proper multicoloring of the graph, satisfying the demand, from a fixed list of \(t\) colors. It is known that all (finite, simple) graphs are Hall \(t\)-chromatic for each \(t\in\{0,1,2\}\), and there is a class of graphs, including the odd wheels except for \(W_3=K_4\), each of which is Hall \(t\)-chromatic only for \(t\in\{0,1,2\}\). \par We show that the Petersen graph is Hall 3-chromatic. Also, by adding a requirement to Hall's \(t\)-condition, we define weak Hall \(t\)-chromaticity and determine for each odd wheel the values of \(t\) for which the wheel is weakly Hall \(t\)-chromatic.
